blocks.text: [III, 32] It is now worth knowing why the Syriac renders the Hebrew תנשמת as ܟܘܟܒܝ cocabi, which at first sight will seem to mean ἀστερίαν [asterian], starry, because ܟܘܟܒ cocab is ἄστρον [astron], star; and the name ἀστερίας [asterias] is common to many birds. For sometimes it is an epithet of the larger eagle, which others call chrysaëtos. Aelian, History of Animals, book 2, chapter 39, [col. 287] Ἀκούω δέ τι καὶ γένος αἰετῶν, καὶ ὄνομα αὐτῶν χρυσαίετον ἔθεντο· ἄλλοι δὲ ἀςερίαν τὸν αὐτὸν καλοῦσιν [Akouō de ti kai genos aietōn, kai onoma autōn chrysaieton ethento; alloi de asterian ton auton kalousin]. So also Michael Apostolius, Century 2, Proverb 6. Sometimes it is a kind of hawk. Thus in Aristotle, History of Animals, book 9, chapter 36, among the species of hawks, after the buteo, the aesalon and the circus, the fourth is reckoned ὁ ἀςερίας [ho asterias]. It is also among the kinds of heron. Aristotle, book 9, chapter 11: Τῶν δ᾽ ἐρωδιῶν ἐςὶ τρία γένη· ὅτε πέλλος, καὶ ὁ λευκὸς, καὶ ὁ ἀςερίας καλούμενος [Tōn d’ erōdiōn esti tria genē; ho te pellos, kai ho leukos, kai ho asterias kaloumenos]. Hence Pliny, book 10, chapter 60: “Of little herons there are three kinds, the leucon, the asterias, the pellos.” Aelian too, History of Animals, book 5, chapter 36, which begins thus: Ὄνομά ἐςιν ὄρνιθος ἀςερίας [Onoma estin ornithos asterias], etc. There are therefore several birds of this name. Indeed, all birds that are painted and marked with spots like stars are called asteriae, or starry. Accordingly, since asterias is an epithet of many birds, it will be difficult to determine which one in particular the Syriac designates by the word ܟܘܟܒܝ cocabi, if indeed it means starry. What of the fact that ܟܘܟܒܝ Cocabi itself can also mean Cocabene, that is, born at Cocaba? There are several towns of this name in Syria and Arabia. One is in Basanitis, of which Epiphanius speaks in the Nazaraeans, writing that their sect flourished ἐν τῇ Βασανίτιδι τῇ λεγομένῃ Κωκάβῃ, Κωχάβῃ δὲ Ἑβραϊςί [en tē Basanitidi tē legomenē Kōkabē, Kōchabē de Hebraisti]. And in the Ebionites: Ἄρχεται μὲν τὴν κατοίκησιν ἔχειν ἐν Κωκάβῃ τινὶ κώμῃ ἐπὶ τὰ μέρη τῆς Καρναΐμ, Ἀρνὲμ, καὶ Ἀςαρὼθ ἐν τῇ Βασανίτιδι χώρᾳ [Archetai men tēn katoikēsin echein en Kōkabē tini kōmē epi ta merē tēs Karnaim, Arnem, kai Astarōth en tē Basanitidi chōra]. And below: Ἀπὸ Μωαβίτιδός τε, καὶ Κωχάβων τῆς ἐν τῇ Βασανίτιδι, ἐπέκεινα Ἀδραῶν [Apo Mōabitidos te, kai Kōchabōn tēs en tē Basanitidi, epekeina Adraōn]. And in the Archontics, of Eutactus, the founder of the sect: Κατῴκησεν ἐν τῇ Ἀραβίᾳ ἐν Κωχάβῃ, ἔνθα αἱ τῶν Ἐβιωναίων τε καὶ Ναζωραίων ῥίζαι ἐνήρξαντο [Katōkēsen en tē Arabia en Kōchabē, entha hai tōn Ebiōnaiōn te kai Nazōraiōn rhizai enērxanto]. There are other Cochabeni, or Cauchabeni, in Arabia Deserta, of whom Ptolemy speaks, book 5, chapter 19: Κατέχουσι δὲ τῆς ἐρήμου ταύτης Ἀραβίας, τὰ μὲν παρὰ τὸν Εὐφράτην ποταμὸν Καυχαβηνοί [Katechousi de tēs erēmou tautēs Arabias, ta men para ton Euphratēn potamon Kauchabēnoi]. And a little after: Ὑπὸ μὲν τοῖς Καυχαβηνοῖς Αἰσῖται [Hypo men tois Kauchabēnois Aisitai]. There is also in the valley of Damascus the town كوكبا [Kawkabā] Caucaba, which the Nubian Geographer mentions, Clim. 3, section 5. And in Alcamus كوكب [Kawkab] Caucab is a fortress of Tiberias, and كوكبان [Kawkabān] Caucaban one of Arabia Iemamitica. Some bird originating from such a place could therefore have been called כוכבי cocabi, or caucabi. Yet we conjecture something else, namely that כוכבי cocabi is the little owl, and that the Syriac translator here agrees with the Chaldees, for whom תנשמת thinsemeth is אותיא, otus, or בותא, eagle owl, birds very like the little owl. This [III, 33] conjecture of ours rests on the following reasons. Little owls are said to cucubare [hoot]. The author of the Philomela:
“The light-shunning little owl hoots in the darkness.”

And Aristophanes in the Birds expresses the song of little owls by the doubled sound κικκαβαῦ, κικκαβαῦ [kikkabau, kikkabau]. And the birds themselves are called κικκαβαὶ [kikkabai], as the Scholiast has there: Κικκαβαῦ) τὰς γλαῦκας οὕτω φωνεῖν λέγουσιν, ὅθεν καὶ κικκαβὰς αὐτὰς λέγουσιν [Kikkabau) tas glaukas houtō phōnein legousin, hothen kai kikkabas autas legousin]. Others prefer κοκκοβὰς [kokkobas]. Hesychius: κοκκοβάρη· γλαύξ [kokkobarē; glaux]. Read instead: Κοκκοβά· ἡ γλαύξ [Kokkoba; hē glaux]. It is also written Κουκουβὰ [Koukouba], whence κουκουβαΐαι [koukoubaiai], glauci fish, because they are of the same colour as τῇ γλαῦκι [tē glauki], that is, the little owl. The Scholiast of Oppian on line 170 of book 1 of the Halieutica: Γλαυκοί· αἱ κουκουβαΐαι [Glaukoi; hai koukoubaiai]. Hence it is very likely that the Syriac ܟܘܟܒܝ cocabi here stands for the little owl ^{(3)}. But I think that the Samaritan ࠒࠐࠅࠐࠄ kaphupha also belongs here, as does the Chaldee קפופא kephupha. So the two Chaldees, the Syriac and the Samaritan understand nearly the same thing by the Hebrew word תנשמת thinsemeth.
